name: Context Engineering for Agents (LangChain blog + filesystem post)
publisher: LangChain (langchain.com / blog.langchain.com) - commercial AI agent infrastructure vendor, maker of LangGraph, LangSmith, and the Deep Agents SDK
date_published: "Context Engineering for Agents" published July 2, 2025 at https://www.langchain.com/blog/context-engineering-for-agents (redirects from blog.langchain.com/context-engineering-for-agents/). "How agents can use filesystems for context engineering" published November 21, 2025 at https://www.langchain.com/blog/how-agents-can-use-filesystems-for-context-engineering, authored by Nick Huang.
claim_value: Two linked claims. (1) A four-strategy taxonomy for agent context engineering: Write (save information outside the context window, e.g. scratchpads/memories), Select (pull relevant information into context, e.g. RAG/memory retrieval), Compress (reduce tokens via summarization/trimming), Isolate (split context across multi-agent architectures or sandboxes). (2) The filesystem follow-up claims a filesystem is the right interface for implementing these strategies in practice, citing four concrete uses: offloading large tool outputs (e.g. web search results) to files and re-reading only relevant excerpts to fight token bloat; writing plans and subagent outputs to files to scale beyond context limits; using ls/glob/grep/read_file for precise retrieval in structured technical docs instead of semantic search; and having agents write feedback-derived instructions back to files for adaptive learning.
claim_definition: A vendor's practitioner framework/technique recommendation, not an original empirical benchmark. Both posts synthesize and re-label prior public work (Karpathy's context-as-RAM analogy, Cognition AI's '#1 job' framing, Anthropic's multi-agent research and agent-skills work, Manus's recitation/filesystem pattern, Cursor's search blog, and explicitly Drew Breunig's four-failure-mode taxonomy and six-tactic list) into a LangChain-branded framework, then maps that framework onto LangChain's own products (LangGraph, LangSmith, Deep Agents SDK).
evidence_category: marketing assertion with embedded citations to others' practitioner anecdotes and (secondhand) benchmark figures; not itself a new benchmark/empirical result
reproducibility: Not an empirical/benchmark claim of LangChain's own, so classic reproducibility doesn't apply directly. However, LangChain published a companion GitHub repo, langchain-ai/how_to_fix_your_context, that implements Breunig's six tactics (RAG, Tool Loadout, Context Quarantine, Pruning, Summarization, Offloading) as runnable LangGraph Jupyter notebooks. The repo's own README states: "Drew Breunig outlined 6 context engineering techniques ... we implement each of these techniques in a set of Jupyter notebooks using LangGraph," explicitly crediting Breunig as the source of the taxonomy being operationalized. The repo was later archived (read-only) as of March 27, 2026.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: Yes. LangChain sells LangGraph (agent orchestration framework), LangSmith (observability/eval platform), and the open-source Deep Agents SDK. Both posts end with explicit calls to action promoting these products as the implementation path for the context engineering patterns described; the filesystem post in particular frames Deep Agents' filesystem tools as the productized version of the pattern it just described.
conflict_notes: LangChain's own GitHub repo is transparent about derivation: it names Breunig directly and states it is implementing his taxonomy. But the two blog posts themselves present "context engineering" as a LangChain-defined discipline (Write/Select/Compress/Isolate is LangChain's own four-way split, not Breunig's), with Breunig's four failure modes (poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash) and six tactics folded in mid-article as supporting citations rather than foregrounded as the taxonomy's origin. A reader who only sees the blog posts (not the GitHub repo) is more likely to credit LangChain with originating the failure-mode vocabulary than a reader who finds the repo. No numeric/statistical discrepancy was found between LangChain's citations and Breunig's original figures in the material reviewed.
relationship: Supports the "prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now" framing explicitly and enthusiastically, citing Cognition AI's claim that context engineering is effectively the #1 job for agent builders and Karpathy's context-as-operating-system-RAM analogy. Both posts treat context engineering as a settled successor discipline to prompt engineering rather than complicating or contradicting that narrative.
derivative_of: Directly derivative of Drew Breunig's essays "How Long Contexts Fail" (June 22, 2025) and "How to Fix Your Context" (June 26, 2025) for the four-failure-mode taxonomy (poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash) and the six-tactic list (RAG, Tool Loadout, Context Quarantine, Pruning, Summarization, Offloading) - named and cited in the main blog post, and explicitly operationalized in the companion GitHub repo (langchain-ai/how_to_fix_your_context). Also cites Andrej Karpathy (context-as-RAM framing), Cognition AI (context engineering as top job), Anthropic (multi-agent researcher system, agent skills), and, for the filesystem post, Manus's "context engineering for AI agents" post and Cursor's search-architecture blog. LangChain's own original contribution is primarily the Write/Select/Compress/Isolate packaging and the product tie-in, not the underlying failure/fix taxonomy.
register: practitioner/engineer primary audience, with enterprise IT buyer undertones via the LangSmith observability/evaluation pitch at the end of both posts
notes: Content for both LangChain posts and the GitHub repo was retrieved via automated fetch-and-summarize rather than a full manual line-by-line read of raw HTML, so exact wording of attributions and the precise ordering of citations within each post have not been independently re-verified beyond the summarized excerpts. The core finding, that LangChain's taxonomy is substantially built on Breunig's prior public work and that LangChain's own repo admits this, is corroborated across three independent fetches (both blog posts, plus the GitHub README) and is consistent with Simon Willison's and others' public commentary tracing the lineage back to Breunig.
new_angle: article_ideas.md's existing 09-27 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' entry cites a different data point (a 2026 industry survey claiming 82% of IT/data leaders say prompts alone no longer suffice) and argues a counterpoint about prompt precision as a design skill; it does not reference LangChain or Breunig by name. This research adds the specific provenance chain: LangChain's popular context-engineering framing is largely a repackaging of Drew Breunig's independently-coined failure taxonomy and six-tactic framework, confirmed by LangChain's own GitHub repo credit line, which is a sharper and more concrete angle for a piece on who actually originates 'context engineering' ideas versus who popularizes and monetizes them.
